Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

Nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he currently co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

Recent findings suggest that what viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he states. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

According to recent reports, how's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

It has been revealed that overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

For the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

But it's been really exciting to just be like, "Oh, we already have three kids, and it only took two pregnancies." So easy for me to say, obviously, but it's been really fun.

Industry observers note that well, congratulations. The first question I have is just wondering what kind of dad are you?

I'm a pretty involved dad and pretty hands-on. Natalie and I, ever since we've been together, we just share the responsibilities of our household. And that was true even before we became parents. I was lucky enough to have the parents I had. And I think that the biggest takeaway I had from my childhood is just how my parents worked as a team.

I have 10 brothers and sisters. And my parents were very lower middle class, very blue collar. My mom stayed home and worked. I mean, my mom stayed home and raised the kids, my dad worked, but that wasn't based on some kind of a decision they made. It was more like that was the situation they had.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of the day-to-day, they shared their responsibility. My mom did a lot of the traditional day-to-day keeping up the house, but my dad would often make dinner. My mom sometimes would mow the lawn. It was just more like all hands on deck type of thing, and you just do things as a team. And that's just something Natalie and I implemented into our relationship early on. And then, obviously, when River showed up, it continued. And then Natalie started working with me on the show.

And so really we're just very involved. And so any little thing I can do to help Natalie or just be an involved parent, we're doing things together every step of the way.

Industry observers note that so I'm just hyper-involved. There's no her thing, my thing. We conquer and divide, and certainly, we joke where I'm allergic to laundry, she's allergic to dishes. I don't mind doing dishes. She doesn't mind doing laundry. So there's definitely things that we have our preferences, but for the most part, we just share everything.

Nick Viall and Natalie Joy Viall have many joint ventures including, namely, the uber-successful Viall Files relationship advice podcast.

What's one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood or will have?

It has been revealed that well, I feel very fortunate to say that I was lucky enough to try to be able to give the best part of my childhood to my children because I was lucky enough to buy back my grandfather's lake house a couple years ago. And that was a place that in my childhood was like my Nirvana. It was my special place.

In a recent development, sadly, when my grandfather passed away when I was in the fourth grade, they sold that property, and it was like this devastating moment of my life. It was like some real childhood trauma.

According to recent reports, and it was a place that, quite frankly, I had recurring dreams all the way into adulthood. And again, I was lucky enough to buy it back and just really excited that it will be a place that I'll hopefully be able to give to my children, and a place that they'll be able to grow up and we'll have, obviously, a lot of hopefully monumental family events there. So that's definitely something I want them to have.

Recent findings suggest that but thinking in the vein of how times might be different, I think the world's changing so fast. I have such fond memories of going to the movies as a child, going to Blockbuster and picking on a movie and things like that. And some of those moments I hope we'll still be able to do. Or just maybe I hope there's a renaissance of people wanting to get outside, touch grass type of thing. And I hope that's something our children will be able to enjoy.

In a recent development, and certainly, in the lake houses up in the middle of nowhere in Wisconsin will be a great tool to help our kids want to be outside and play in nature and just make-believe. Most of my childhood was a lot of just make believe with my friends outside. And we would ride our bikes all over the place.

According to recent reports, it's weird. I'm sure you're probably familiar with that book, The Anxious Generation by Jonathan … he talked about the freedoms that kids used to have back in the day and parents like 5, 10 years ago got a little... it's like you get nervous about the world, but you took for granted, again, the dangers of the phone. And so I'm really hoping my kids get to embrace the world and get outside and play make believe with their friends and things like that. So that's a big focus for us and certainly, hopefully, something that I hope they do get to enjoy because those are always fond memories that I have as a child.

Recent findings suggest that that's a great perspective. I mean, I do agree that right now is a good time to have kids because everyone is much more aware of the difficulties parents are facing . You'll see all the support in elementary school. It's really talked about a lot.

And on to the next question: What does your wife love about you?

Sources indicate that well, I think probably just the fact that, I hope, that I like to think I'm her rock. There's so much burden and pressure on moms postpartum. I like to think that my job is just to be a cheerleader. When I get a sense that she's stressed out or feeling overwhelmed, I'm quick to try to give her a break, tell her to go lie down if that's what she wants to do. I'm always there and always available.

According to recent reports, and I hope that's one thing that she loves most about me, but I just try to be as supportive as possible just to remind her and just be a cheerleader. Just always remind her that she's doing a great job because, again, there's just so much pressure that moms put on themselves.

The other side of that coin, what does she maybe find annoying about you?

Oh, my God, the list is so long. Well, I don't know how to close a cupboard. I don't put things away. I leave a trail of destruction wherever I go. I'm messier than our two-year-old. So there is that.

Sources indicate that I've recently got back into some video game playing, which definitely gives her the ick, but she is kind enough to let me decompress with a game here or there. So I think she'd prefer it not to exist, but … everything in moderation. Again, the trick for any dad out there who enjoys a video game or two is to never let it get in the way of being helpful. So that's the trick to get it in when you can, but never let it come in the way of, obviously, being a partner and being a father.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

In a recent development, I mean, it means everything to me. I've had this conversation with a lot of peers that I have, and I have a lot of women friends in the space I work in, and so talked to some latest young mothers, young professionals who, obviously, their careers are and still are really important to them.

It has been revealed that once you have a child, I describe it as the easiest North Star. I've been fortunate enough in my life to accomplish a lot of cool things and it's nice to have individual accomplishments and accolades and awards, but they're not always as fulfilling as you think they might be when they happen. Fatherhood, parenthood is just... you always know why you're doing something. You always know what the purpose is. And so even the late nights, it's a drag to get up at 2:00 in the morning, but you know why you're doing it, and you always get a sense of purpose and accomplishment. And it's just the best motivator. No matter what's going on in work or in our personal life, it really calms you down.

I'm a fairly anxious, high-stress guy. It's easy for me to get worried about work and all the things that are going on in this world. And then I have the benefit of coming home, and especially with River now when she greets me. I'm constantly on my phone with work, and I'm never not working in a sense, but when I walk into the house, Natalie's incorporated this kind of best practice of making sure I'm off my phone and I'm very present to greet River. Even if it's for a few minutes, even if I still have some work left to do, I never walk in on the phone and I'm not giving her my undivided attention. And it's something like Natalie incorporated, which I really appreciate that she did, and I think it's just a really great best practice that we do.

Thank you so much for all the thoughtful answers.

It has been revealed that I appreciate it, man. It's fun to talk about fatherhood.

Sources indicate that it's something I really enjoy. And it's weird because in my... I don't know if you've noticed this. I mean, it's weird how parenting has become, like everything else these days, almost like a polarizing topic. No parent is indifferent about parenting, and obviously, every parent comes with passion, but it's weirdly become a topic that I'd want to talk about more, but sometimes it's like you want to be careful because you don't want to force your thoughts and feelings onto others.

In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a fresh building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school.

In a recent development, when my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a major deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day?

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the plan because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

According to recent reports, luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

In a recent development, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by the USDA and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) every five years. When the DGA gets an patch, school nutrition standard changes will follow, as required by law.

Schools are currently implementing changes developed following the release of the 2020-2025 DGA. In April 2024, the Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA, formerly Food and Nutrition Service) , a government agency responsible for administering domestic nutrition programs, like the NSLP, issued a rule requiring schools to make changes to foods served at school, including:.

These updates join a comprehensive list of nutrition standards for school breakfasts and lunches that outline weekly serving requirements for fruits, vegetables, grains, meats and meat alternatives, and milk, as well as calorie minimums and maximums, and limits on saturated fat.

In a recent development, the USDA and HHS released the 2025-2030 DGA on January 7, 2026, triggering the next wave of school nutrition reviews in preparation for new recommendations and requirements. The USDA will compare the new DGA guidelines against existing school nutrition requirements, then draft a proposed rule on which schools, state agencies, advocates, industry experts, and consumer advocacy groups, like Center for the Science in the Public Interest, can provide feedback. The USDA will read and respond to comments, sometimes changing planned provisions in response to the feedback received, then publish its final rule.

At face value, this may seem like a good thing.

Industry observers note that the USDA and HHS appoints a Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee (DGAC) every five years to serve as an independent, expert panel of scientists and researchers in nutrition, health and medicine. The committee spends years reviewing current nutrition science to write a scientific report that’s typically used as a foundational resource for new dietary guidelines. DGAs have historically followed the vast majority of the DGAC’s recommendations. But, as CSPI notes, USDA and HHS rejected more than half of the DGAC’s expert recommendations. Instead, the agencies, according to CSPI,  “hand-picked authors whose work aligned with beef, dairy, and protein supplement industry interests and the administration’s preconceived policy goals.”.

This group of hand-picked authors created a new “Scientific Foundation for Dietary Guidelines for Americans,” which includes contradictory advice, recommending folks stick to prior, science-based saturated fat limits, while suggesting high-fat foods like whole milk and beef tallow are part of a healthy diet.

CSPI has raised other concerns about the 2025-2030 DGA, arguing that it gives harmful guidance to emphasize animal protein; advises people to consume double or more of the scientifically-backed recommendation for daily protein; reduces clarity around how people can eat a balanced diet within vegetable and protein categories; and adopts an inverted food pyramid that doesn’t accurately visually represent the dietary recommendations found within the text of the guidelines.

As in cycles past, schools expect the USDA to use the most recent DGA as a guide to propose changes to school nutrition standards. It’s unclear exactly what changes will be put forth, but there will likely be a mix of nutrition wins and losses. It’s possible the new standards will reflect evidence-based nutrition guidance like increasing whole grains, protein, and whole fruit, and cutting back on added sugars, sodium, and refined grains in school meals.

In a recent development, however, it’s also likely the latest proposed standards may stray from evidence-based guidance by calling for decreased vegetable variety and overall fiber intake due to a deprioritization of plant-based proteins and an overemphasis on high-fat foods like whole milk and beef (rather than a variety of protein sources). For example, students could see more protein, like eggs and yogurt, at breakfast but miss out on a rainbow of vegetables and inclusive protein options like beans and tofu at lunch. Zooming out, meals lower in added sugars could be prioritized, while progress made on reducing saturated fat and sodium in school meals will be lost.

Sources indicate that the best way to inform what your kids get on their breakfast and lunch trays at school is to make your voice heard. After proposing changes to nutrition standards, the government will open a public comment period where you can share your opinions about what should be included or excluded from school meals. When the proposed rule finally comes out, CSPI will make it easy to share your opinion through model comments and templates that will allow parents to comment directly on the proposed rule. Stay tuned for next steps by signing up for CSPI advocacy emails.

According to recent reports, the regulatory red tape may seem overwhelming. That’s why non-profits like CSPI give parents tools to learn about school nutrition standards and enact change. To learn more about school nutrition standards, visit CSPI’s Healthier School Food advocacy page. If you’re ready to advocate for healthier school meals, check out CPSI’s Take Action page to get involved.

Industry News: How to Winterize an Outdoor Faucet – This 5-Minute Job Could Save You Thousands

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture a hose still screwed onto the spigot in December.
  • It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers.
  • Sources indicate that outdoor faucet winterization is mostly about getting water out and keeping it from getting trapped again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture a hose still screwed onto the spigot in December. The water behind it has nowhere to go. Once nights stay below 32°F (0°C), it can freeze solid, and copper and brass don't have much give. Something splits. That repair bill usually runs well past what the faucet cost, so it pays to sort out how to winterize an outdoor faucet now.

It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers. The annoying part is where the damage hides. From the yard, the faucet can look fine while the pipe behind it has cracked a few inches inside the wall. Nobody sees that until the water's back on.

Sources indicate that outdoor faucet winterization is mostly about getting water out and keeping it from getting trapped again. Take off the hose, shut off the supply, drain what's left, and add a cover for backup. Try to finish alongside your other gardening winterizing tasks, and before the first hard freeze shows up in the forecast.

Recent findings suggest that if you only get to one step today, make it this one. Any hose left on the spigot holds water inside the faucet, and that goes for frost-free models too – the water has nowhere to drain while the hose is attached. Splitters, watering timers, and quick-connect fittings trap water the same way, so pull them all off.

Industry observers note that then empty the hose. Stretch it down a slope or drape loops over a fence rail so the water runs out both ends. Leftover water can freeze and split it, and a drained hose stored out of the weather generally holds up longer. Suncast's 100-foot Hose Hideaway from Walmart keeps a coiled hose off the ground under a lid.

Start inside. Standard faucets usually have their own shutoff, somewhere close to where the pipe goes out through the wall, often in a basement, crawl space, or utility room. Look up between the ceiling joists, too. A round handle turns clockwise until it stops. If it's a lever, a quarter turn puts it crosswise to the pipe, and that's closed.

Industry observers note that not every home has one, and older houses often don't, which makes it harder to winterize hose bib lines without shutting off water to the whole house. If you're not sure what an unlabeled valve is, leave it alone. Close the wrong one, and it's no fun to find out halfway through washing dishes. Frost-free faucets, like this SharkBite one, work differently and may not need this step.

For faucets without a dedicated indoor shutoff, a Freeze Miser outdoor faucet protector offers another option. It screws onto the spigot and automatically releases a small amount of water when the water temperature drops below 37°F (3°C), helping prevent freezing. Unlike conventional winterizing, this method requires leaving the water supply on and the outdoor faucet fully open.

Head back outside and open the faucet all the way. Some water should run out, slow to a trickle, and stop. Did it keep flowing? Then the indoor valve isn't closed all the way, or it's not the right valve at all.

It has been revealed that some shutoffs have a little cap on the side, called a bleeder. Leave the outdoor faucet open so air can get in, set a bucket underneath, and back the cap off slowly. Water will dribble out. When it quits, screw the cap back on. Many plumbers will leave the outdoor faucet open all winter. Some valve makers say to close it, though, so go by whatever came with yours.

An outdoor faucet cover holds in a little of the warmth that seeps through the wall from inside. The rigid type (like the image above) is a foam-lined dome with a cord that pulls it snug against the siding. Home Depot's Everbilt hard outdoor faucet cover is a good cheap option. Flexible pouches go on more like a sock (see image below), and the Thinsulate-lined faucet socks on Amazon come two to a pack.

Industry observers note that either kind should sit flat against the wall with no gap for cold air. Check it after windy nights, because covers do get knocked loose. It's backup, not a substitute for unhooking hoses and draining the line, and outdoor spigot winter protection still starts with an empty faucet. An Ambient Weather Wi-Fi weather station can send temperature alerts to your phone before a hard freeze.

It has been revealed that plenty of people hear frost-free and figure that means forget about it. That's about half right, maybe. From the yard, a frost-free outdoor faucet looks like any other spigot. Its handle turns a long stem, and the part that stops the water sits way back at the end of it, where it's warmer. Close it, and the water in that stem should run out the spout. That only works if the faucet slopes a little toward the outside.

So the hose still comes off, or water stays put and can freeze inside the wall, often unnoticed until spring. Damage, a level installation, or a pipe running through an unheated crawl space can leave one vulnerable too.

In a recent development, correctly installed ones usually don't need the supply shut off and drained, but the manufacturer's instructions get the final say. Homes without an indoor shutoff can have a plumber fit a replacement such as the SharkBite one mentioned above.

If the faucet won't run or ice has formed around the spout, skip the torch, even if one happens to be sitting right there in the garage. No open flame, and nothing else that blasts heat at it, either. There's framing and insulation right behind that siding. Hair dryers are slower. Point it at the faucet and the wall around it and give it time. Keep the cord out of puddles.

It has been revealed that suspect a leak? Shut off the water to that line, or the main valve if there's no separate one, and call a plumber. Frozen pipe damage isn't always visible right away. A crack of ⅛ inch (3 mm) can let out up to 250 gallons (946L) a day, and it may not drip at all until the ice thaws or the water goes back on.

Sources indicate that most of what it takes to protect outdoor faucets from freezing – and to prevent frozen pipes behind them – is getting the water out and keeping it out. Get that done before the first hard frost, and the faucet should be ready come spring, with dry walls behind it.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

According to recent reports, but authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future.”.

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

According to recent reports, he also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”.

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

Recent findings suggest that what Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, key for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”.

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most important thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”.

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

You say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

Recent findings suggest that I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

What’s your wife love about you?

I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

It has been revealed that she doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

It has been revealed that I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A big part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

Recent findings suggest that she knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

My first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

So you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

#228140. Breaking: Her friend died after giving birth. Now she’s writing legislation to save other moms

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1258 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mother ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Her friend died after giving birth. Now she’s writing legislation to save other moms

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change.
  • In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a major, bright smile named Shalon Irving.
  • Recent findings suggest that she never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change. Each piece is part of a larger effort to ensure every mother and family in the U.S. has the support and care to be well.

In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a major, bright smile named Shalon Irving.

Recent findings suggest that she never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work. Underwood would eventually become a U.S. representative for the state of Illinois, fighting to protect moms like Irving, who died before she could see her friend take office.

At the time, Irving, who already had her PhD, was coming back to school for additional training in public health. “We were just like regular girlfriends, passing notes in class and everything,” Rep. Underwood indicates.

Industry observers note that the two—Rep. Underwood, a registered nurse, and Irving, an epidemiologist—stayed in touch through the years. In January 2017, Rep. Underwood served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and Irving worked for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She had also given birth to a beautiful baby girl named Soleil.

Three weeks later, though, Irving wasn’t feeling well. “She went to the doctor several times, explaining that something wasn’t right,” Rep. Underwood remembers. On January 28, Irving died of complications related to high blood pressure. She was 36.

“Shalon had a career focused on ending health disparities, and she was so excited to become a mom,” Rep. Underwood claims.

Today, Rep. Underwood is the architect of a series of 14 bills called the Momnibus, which was reintroduced to Congress this spring. The Momnibus addresses “every clinical and non-clinical factor” leading to preventable maternal deaths and disparities in this country; it’s evidence-based, data-driven, and offers states, communities, providers, and nonprofits the resources to help save moms like Irving’s lives. For Rep. Underwood, the Momnibus is personal.

Recent findings suggest that while a member of Congress, Rep. Underwood is also a woman and a friend who, like too many in this country, lost a dear friend and felt a fire to make change.

Rep. Underwood recalls Irving’s funeral as devastating—particularly because many of those in attendance held positions of the highest authority in public health in this country. She remembers the head of the CDC speaking at Irving’s funeral and expressing bewilderment at her death.

It has been revealed that for Rep. Underwood, it was no mystery why mothers like Irving die in childbirth and shortly thereafter. As a clinician, she had seen firsthand health disparities in action; as a Black woman, maternal mortality was an unfortunate “phenomenon where it’s just so common when you talk about the maternal crisis.”.

Today, we know about 84 percent of pregnancy-related deaths like Irving’s are preventable—meaning that most of the moms who aren’t here today should be here, and could be here, with the proper supports in place. Black moms are more than three times as likely to die in pregnancy or the postpartum months than white women—a disparity that persists across income and education levels.

“People think higher education or higher income is protective. They think that if you are a healthcare worker, you’re going to get the best healthcare. If you know the risks, are self-aware, confident, and have agency, and you can speak up for yourself, then these kinds of things won’t happen to you. Shalon and her death fly in the face of all of those assumptions, and it breaks your heart.”.

It has been revealed that when she made the decision to run for Congress, Rep. Underwood knew that if she won, maternal mortality would be an issue she’d work on.

Industry observers note that in 2018, Rep. Underwood became the youngest Black woman ever elected to Congress. She teamed up with Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC), who also had personal experience with maternal health: Adams’ daughter had experienced a very challenging labor and delivery, known in medical terms as severe maternal morbidity, or an experience that has lasting impacts on a mother’s health.

Together, in April 2019, the two formed the Black Maternal Health Caucus. At a crowded press conference, Rep. Underwood fought back tears. “To be in this moment with the dome of the Capitol behind us and these cameras and people asking questions and it’s this diverse, multi-generational, multi-ethnic, male and female moment of speaking about an issue that was so personal to me—I was just overcome,” she indicates. “It was a moment of power and resolve. It was an invitation. We were planting a flag, saying, ‘We’re here. We’re going to do this work. We know that there’s an opportunity to bring change.’”.

Industry observers note that rep. Underwood didn’t expect the Black Maternal Health Caucus to grow into one of the largest bipartisan caucuses on the Hill. “We left that press conference and our phones started ringing, and it never stopped.”.

Sources indicate that rep. Underwood has dedicated her career to ensuring everyone—moms included—has equitable healthcare so we can all feel our best. She’s also dedicated her career to ending the maternal mortality crisis. “We know exactly what to do. We just need to invest, have the resolve, and to say, ‘This is unacceptable. Let’s fix this glitch.’”.

It has been revealed that she also reminds us that Congress works on the issues that members raise. “If a Member comes in and says, ‘This is key to my community, and this is an essential issue that we tackle,’ that’s how solutions advance.” Many of her ideas for bills, she says, come from your stories.

It has been revealed that “Often, people think that their story doesn’t matter, and when they come in to advocate, they think they need to have statistics or be a walking encyclopedia,” Rep. Underwood says. “But we are in a relationship business, and connection is currency. The fastest way to build a connection is to share your humanity, tell your story, and invite space for that vulnerability.”.

In a recent development, what that means for you: If you have a story to share, Members of Congress are home in their districts through the end of the month, with offices open Monday through Friday and available for meetings. (Not sure how to set up a meeting? Check out Chamber of Mothers’ ‘Moms at Recess’ guide, which includes step-by-step plans and tips for hosting a meeting with Members of Congress.).

Sources indicate that rep. Underwood also underscores the importance of being loud about solutions and progress in maternal health. She highlights the power of doulas, lactation consultants, and community support in maternal health—and the fact that, to date, one of the Momnibus’ 14 bills has been signed into law. Others have passed the House. The Momnibus has also unlocked more than $250 million for states, community organizations, researchers, and providers to save lives. (You can find out which projects are being funded with Momnibus dollars in your community through the Caucus’s Momnibus Money Tracker.).

“We want the news of a pregnancy to be a time of joy and hope and eager anticipation and wonder,” Rep. Underwood notes. “This can’t just be a conversation around problems. We want people to know that we’re working on this, that we have their backs, and about the opportunities, help, and the resources that are available.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AJ McLean, the singer, songwriter, and most tattooed member of The Backstreet Boys just moved his family to New York City.
  • Industry observers note that but before he can take the family to the Rockettes, McLean has an album to launch (Sex, Love, and Music, out Nov.
  • Industry observers note that I think I am a cool dad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just one of the Boys raising two girls.

Industry observers note that AJ McLean, the singer, songwriter, and most tattooed member of The Backstreet Boys just moved his family to New York City. “All three of the ladies in my life love New York,” he says — and he’s all about it. “Celebrating Christmas in New York this year is going to be fantastic.”.

Industry observers note that but before he can take the family to the Rockettes, McLean has an album to launch (Sex, Love, and Music, out Nov. 27) and a solo tour to rock (The Better Man Tour). He is also busy as the spokesman for Delsym 12-Hour Cough Relief, which he states saved a performance during The Backstreet Boys residency at The Sphere last year. McLean took a break from his tour to take Fatherly’s Cool Dad questionnaire — and talk about staying healthy, sober, and putting family first.

Industry observers note that I think I am a cool dad. I think I'm a cool dad because I really kind of let my kids form their own opinions and have a voice, and we work as a team. I want my girls to always have a voice. That's super vital to me. Sometimes, they have too much of a voice, but it's OK. That's when dad has to step in and reel it back a little bit. I want my girls to just always look up to their dad, and I try to set the best example that I can.

AJ McLean on his solo “The Better Man” Tour.

What's the best film to watch with kids?

Industry observers note that so I'm an ’80s kid and I am so happy that I turned my girls onto Labyrinth, which they absolutely love; The Goonies, which they absolutely love; and Gremlins. They are obsessed, especially with Labyrinth. When I mentioned it to them, they were a little hesitant, and then once we watched it, I went back to work and caught wind from the wife that they've watched it repeatedly days after, and I'm like, "Yes, I did it.".

What's one thing you wish your kids had today that you had growing up, especially as a kid from the ’80s?

I wish they had cassette tape players. I did get a cassette tape player gift box from my boys over at Aerosmith, and it came with a cassette tape of their latest album — it was a promotional thing. And I demonstrated it to my daughters, and they did not know what they were looking at. They put it in backwards. I'm like, "No, no, no, no, no, no." And then they were like, "What is the red button?" I stated, "No, that's for recording." And they were astounded when I pressed play and this little speaker was playing and I'm like, "When your dad was growing up, that was it. That's all we had. There was no Bose surround sound, there was none of that.".

Industry observers note that and then my youngest — last year as a birthday present from one of her friends — got a Discman. And she of course put the CD in upside down, I had to show her the right way. That was painful. But she really loves her freaking Discman. She loves it. And I love that they're starting to come back where you actually have to buy the CD. I keep telling my girls, "There's pictures in there; there's thank yous; there's a whole thing. It's not just listening to the music; it's a whole package deal, where you don't get that if you're listening to iTunes. You see one picture and listen to the music, that's it. Albums were a thing." So I'm starting to get them into that now, which I really love.

What's music have you successfully introduced your kids to?

My oldest daughter's first album was The Beatles’ White Album. She learned every word between the ages of 2 and 3. And she was a sponge. My wife is the biggest Beatles fan out of anyone I've ever met in my life. She is diehard. So that was her first album. She's like, "This is what my kids are listening to, Beatles." I'm like, "OK.".

AJ McLean and his family, pictured here in 2022, recently moved to New York City.

And what music have your kids introduced you to?

Recently, I took the family to the premiere of Michael, and my daughters knew who Michael Jackson was, but after the film, the obsession was over the top. They know songs I've never heard, deep cuts. People forget about Michael's Jackson’s Xscape album and they're saying, "Dad, play such and such a song." And I'm like, "That's not a song." They're like, "Yes, it is." They know more music, I think, now than I've ever known in my entire life. We have a very musical family, very musical family.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

Fatherhood, to me, means protection. It means compassion, understanding. It means listening with my ears and not my mouth, and being nonjudgmental, which I'm a very nonjudgmental person anyways, but just by nature, that's how I was raised. And trying to really broaden my daughters’ spectrum of the world, and to love everyone, and to accept everyone, and to be colorblind, to be genderblind, to be just very open and loving. And they are. They are two of the coolest kids I think any father could ever ask for. They are super smart. They are loving kids. They are people, people like me.

According to recent reports, they're not shy by any means. They will talk to everybody and talk their ear off, and I have no idea where they get that from. But yeah, I try to just really set an example, especially as a father and as a man, I want my daughters to look at me and then be able to say when the time comes that they want to date boys, this is what a boy should be. This is what a man should be, like, respectful. And I grew up single-parent household, so I grew up to very much so respect women to the utmost, and put them up on a pedestal, which it's kind of a give and take, but to really know that none of us would be here without a woman, let's just say that.

What piece of clothing or gear are you really passionate about right now? What do you can't get enough of?

I mean, I'm a sneakerhead. I have a problem. And I've gotten my girls into it now, which my wife is so thrilled about.

Industry observers note that well, it's easier for me because I'm done. My foot's where it's at, it ain't going up, it ain't going down, but my daughters are still growing. So when I go get a pair of Jordans that are like $200 and then my kids want to match daddy's shoes, it's a little like they're going to be in them for six months and then they're going to be out of them. But then we donate them anyway, so we're not just throwing them out; we're donating them.

What are you wearing right now then? What's on your feet?

In a recent development, right now, I've got my travel shoes, which are my Adidas Ultraboost, but my everyday shoes are [Jordan] 1s or 3s. That is my go-to. My collection has gotten pretty large. And my daughters now, they're nowhere near as many as me, but they're starting to catch up.

What does Rochelle love about you?

It has been revealed that I think she loves my heart, my generosity, my kindness, my ability to be very comforting and loving. I'm a very affectionate person. I try to be a very loyal person. I try to be a very honest person. I have my faults; nobody's perfect. I tell people I'm perfectly imperfect. And I think she just loves me for me. I think even more so now, being sober for over five years and living my true authentic self, our relationship now I think is the best it's ever been, being in each other's lives for 15 years.

Sources indicate that we went through some tough stuff. We separated, we were living separately, and we both now can look back and reflect on what needed to happen. There are no mistakes. I believe everything happens exactly how it's meant to be. We needed that time apart to grow individually and to grow as a unit. And now, we're living together as a family for the first time in almost four years. We're renting a place in Fresh York so my girls can go to an incredible dance school, and all three of the ladies in my life love New York, and they would've moved there years ago.

They're having the time of their life. And I told them, because we actually moved the tail end of summer, and none of my girls have ever experienced humidity or the heat that is the East Coast.

And I would FaceTime them and be like, "Oh, dear God, what's with your hair?" But now they understand.

Now they know that everyone leaves the city in the summer, so you'll do that next year.

Exactly. But celebrating Christmas in Fresh York this year is going to be fantastic.

So I just got over a cold myself, and it's like, I'm wondering, you're touring, you moved, you travel, you're now in crowded New York, and you have germy kids. Is this why you partnered with Delsym: 12-Hour Cough Relief? How do you deal with the illness, staying healthy, prevention and all that.

I mean, it's pretty crazy because after doing what I do for ... I've been in the business for 40 years. That is how long I've been in the world of entertainment. And I think especially with being with the Boys, my immunity has kind of skyrocketed because of, I think, how much interaction I have with people, but I'm human, and I still do get sick. It's rare, but it does happen, especially being out here on my own. I don't have the boys to lean on. If I go down, I go down. And this is cold and flu season right now, and you're on a tight quarters on a bus. If somebody gets sick, it spreads like wildfire. But for me, two years ago when we first kicked off our residency at Sphere, the second weekend, I got very sick and I was coughing uncontrollably, and that's not an easy show to do if you're not well.

In a recent development, and Delsym is the only product I know works 100%. It's 12 hours of relief that not only does it get me through the show, but it continues after that, because that's really where you feel it. If you're not in a good way, not only are you going to feel it during the show, but afterwards because you're pushing through. But that is my go-to, has been, will always be. Moving forward as an artist, that, I know is my guarantee to get through a show because let's face it, nobody wants to go see a concert and watch their artist cough more than sing, you know what I mean? And especially me out here by myself.

One pick per real-life diaper disaster, from the newborn days to the crawl-away-mid-change era.

Industry observers note that forty years ago, parents had two diaper choices: cloth or disposable. That was kind of it. Now, we have the internet and Reddit opinions and TikTok influencers telling us which diapers they swear by. The list is endless and ripe for an endless 3 a.m. scroll.

According to recent reports, fortunately, you don’t need a PhD in absorbent polymers to pick a diaper; you just need the right one for your baby’s actual problem. So, we ranked the best baby diapers of 2026 by situation.

It has been revealed that the verdict: The best everyday diaper for newborns and beyond... the easiest “just buy this”.

The verdict: The best blowout fix for a baby who treats changes like a contact sport.

The verdict: A nighttime diaper for babies who soak through before morning.

The verdict: A fragrance-free premium pick for skin that reacts to everything.

What’s the best subscription diaper strategy for the money?

Should I use a premium or budget diaper if my baby’s in daycare full-time?

Budget diapers can handle daytime. In Consumer Reports’ 2026 testing, its budget Value Pick scored as high on absorption and dryness as its top performer. Many parents opt for budget during the day and premium for overnight.

Is a thinner or thicker diaper better for an active, cruising toddler?

A slimmer core with a flexible waistband (like Pampers Cruisers 360 Fit) tends to give busy babies more freedom of movement without losing all-important absorbency.

How often should I change a newborn’s diaper to prevent rash?

Changing diapers every 2 to 3 hours and using barrier ointment is the main way to prevent diaper rash, per AAP. If a rash won’t clear up, bleeds, or looks like an allergic reaction, call your pediatrician or dermatologist.

Do I really need a different diaper for day versus night?

Not always, but heavy wetters often do. Separate day and night diapers are an increasingly common fix for overnight soakers. Pampers AMORE, launched in March 2026, is billed by Pampers as its most absorbent diaper, in sizes Newborn-7.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Poinsettias might be the traditional choice for festive decorating, but they're not the only Christmas houseplants capable of bringing a splash of holiday color indoors.

If you're looking for something a little different this year, there is a holiday plant that promises the same bold red hues of a poinsettia, along with glossy succulent leaves and a surprisingly easygoing nature. And no, we're not talking about sweet box (although that's also a brilliant container plant to add to your shopping list).

Instead, we're dragging the beautiful Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) into the spotlight, as its flowers can last for weeks, making it a lovely way to brighten your home through the darker months.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

In a recent development, often sold as a seasonal flowering plant, Flaming Katy is actually a tender perennial succulent, which means you don't necessarily have to throw it away once Christmas is over. In fact, all you have to do is give it the right conditions and it can continue growing for years, potentially rewarding you with another spectacular display.

It has been revealed that there's no denying that poinsettias look impressive, but they can be surprisingly fussy about their surroundings, as they dislike cold draughts and sudden temperature changes – so much so that their leaves can drop. Overwatering is another common problem, particularly when plants are left sitting in decorative pots without adequate drainage.

Flaming Katy offers a much easier alternative, as its leaves store water, helping it cope with occasional dry spells, while its clusters of brightly colored flowers provide plenty of festive impact. Red is a particularly popular choice for Christmas, of course, although you can also find varieties with pink, orange, yellow and white flowers, too.

Recent findings suggest that better still? Rather than providing a brief burst of colour, a healthy plant can remain in bloom for several weeks, sometimes even longer depending on the variety and growing conditions.

In a recent development, unlike some Christmas houseplants, this one doesn't need constant attention to keep looking good. Once you find a suitable position (a birght windowsill is ideal), the main thing is to avoid overwatering and make sure it receives enough light.

It also prefers average indoor humidity, so there's no need to mist it or create a particularly humid environment; in fact, good air circulation is more useful than excessive moisture around the leaves. Just keep it somewhere warm, ideally with temperatures around 60–75°F (16–24°C), and give it plenty of bright, indirect light (and remember that some gentle morning sunshine is generally welcome, too).

During the flowering period, you can remove individual faded flower clusters to keep the plant looking tidy, but there's no need for complicated pruning or constant feeding.

Perhaps the best thing about Flaming Katy is that, even though it's a Christmas houseplant, it doesn't have to be a disposable festive decoration; once flowering finishes, you can continue growing it as a foliage houseplant. With the right care, it can produce newly introduced growth and flower again.

According to recent reports, oh sure, poinsettias will always have their place in Christmas decorating, but Flaming Katy makes a convincing alternative if you'd prefer something colorful, undemanding and potentially longer-lasting when it comes to brightening up a home during winter. And unlike a certain fussy red plant that pops up everywhere in the holidays, this little flowering succulent really can stick around for years.

From custom wrapping paper to cozy matching PJs, these are the gifts worth grabbing before the December scramble.

If there’s one thing that’s wildly helpful to keep in mind heading into this final stretch of the year, it’s that the holidays aren’t just one day.

Recent findings suggest that right now, we’re in the warm-up period, getting ready for what’s ultimately a months-long marathon of hosting, gift-wrapping, card-writing and cozy holiday cheer. So while, sure, there may be bags of half-eaten Halloween candy presently littering your countertops, it’s time to start thinking about the stuff you need to do (and buy) now to max out the holiday merriment and minimize the holiday stress.

What most of us have learned the hard way, of course, is that personalized gifts need a little extra time to make and ship. Placing those orders now gives you the head start you need! But also, why save all the good stuff for December anyway? We here at Scary Mommy are significant believers in gifting early, both to ourselves and the people we love, especially when it’s stuff that’ll get used all season long, like matching PJs for every hot cocoa night and puzzles to work on as the weather turns.

We’ve rounded up what we’re buying now so that the holidays can be more about the fun stuff and less about the December scramble.

It has been revealed that I love the idea of giving personalized wrapping paper at the holidays. It's charming, it's unique, and it's very specific. When else would you do this — and actually use what you buy? — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

It has been revealed that these are very chic little cocktail napkins that make a great hostess gift throughout the holiday season. They come in a variety of patterns, and while, sure, are more than I normally spend on such a thing, they make a nice gift whether you're headed somewhere for cocktails, for Thanksgiving, or beyond. — Kate Auletta.

Forgive me, but I'm at the age where I have more than one doormat. I even have a Halloween one outside right now. It spruces up your outdoor space in a second and makes a nice gift too. I just love coming home to a welcoming doormat; sue me. — Kate Auletta.

If I had a nickel for every personalized notebook I had... I'd have about $3. But still, the point remains: A personalized notebook makes a great gift. You remember who gave it to you as you open it to start using it, and, as someone who is a chronic pen-and-paper girlie, I just love them. They make a great gift year-round, but especially at the holidays. — Kate Auletta.

In a recent development, I have a love-hate relationship with tree skirts. They're incredibly annoying, but incredibly useful. But I do love a tree skirt with character, and this one has it in spades. I love the idea of giving a newborn family a monogrammed tree skirt they can use for years to come. Such a sweet gift! — Kate Auletta.

Industry observers note that I'm a puzzler, especially when it gets cold outside. I love the idea of doing a thick wood, personalized puzzle that will remind you of the moment captured, as well as the person or family who gave it to you. It makes a lovely gift, promise. — Kate Auletta.

Ok, how friggin' cute is this? My kids no longer believe in Santa, but I almost want to buy this for our house. It's a great thing to whip out as the holidays — and the gift requests — amp up. Read their letters and write personalized notes on Christmas Eve while drinking eggnog. Win-win. — Kate Auletta.

It has been revealed that I care about my guest bath maybe more than I care about my own. It's, like, my space. As such, I love the idea of giving monogrammed towels for the space that you can whip out, especially at the holidays. They'll get used, and they're great quality. — Kate Auletta.

Industry observers note that call me a Boomer, but I love switching out throw pillows for each season. And I adore these tree pillows, which are not only affordable but can sit prettily on your couch for months. They're a lovely gift, or if you're feeling selfish, a lovely gift to yourself. — Kate Auletta.

Any house that can pull off an outdoor lights display at the holidays is fine by me. What I love about these is that, sure, you can buy them for the winter holidays, but you can reuse them for Halloween, the Fourth of July, or a random Saturday. They're just so fun, especially if you have kids. You can't go wrong. — Kate Auletta.

In a recent development, one of my absolute most favorite holiday traditions is seasonal PJs! When our kids were little, we would always get them matching sets like these super festive, cozy ones from Magnetic Me. The fact that these feature magnets for easy, over-the-head dressing is a huge bonus. Buy them now so you can be cute and coordinated for every holiday movie night and hot cocoa sipping session. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

Recent findings suggest that white Christmas stans, rise! Old World Christmas hand-blown glass ornaments are genuinely heirloom quality, with that gorgeous old-fashioned detailing and rich color that makes them look like they came from a European Christmas market rather than an online cart. This one is specifically for sisters, which makes it an incredibly thoughtful gift for a sibling, a best friend who is basically a sister, or honestly just yourself if you have a sister you want to think of every time you see it on the tree. The kind of ornament that starts a tradition and gets passed down eventually! — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

We have had so much fun with our mini photo printer from Canon — and it's a perfect thing to get before the holidays get rolling. I love taking pictures during a party or event and then handing out hard copies as our guests go out the door. It's such a good, simple party favor. You can also set up homemade photo booths! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

Do yourself a favor TODAY and buy this Slice tool for cutting wrapping paper. I swear it saved me 7-10 business days while wrapping. I literally hide it from the rest of my family. And while you're at it, buy the Slice box cutter, too. They both make my life easier and happier. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, before the turkey is steaming on your holiday table... before you need to chop one thousand vegetables for the party, run every knife in your kitchen through this electric knife sharpener. I bring this baby out right before the holidays start and sharpen everything that isn't nailed down in my kitchen, and it almost feels like self-care. Using a sharp knife makes so much more of a difference than you think! — Sarah Aswell.

Recent findings suggest that this is what I've been looking for! I love having cafe lights strung up around my porch for entertaining during the summer — what if they could just MAGICALLY turn into holiday lights for Halloween and then Christmas? Now they can. These programmable lights mean that I am not constantly putting up and taking down lights — the colors just change with the season, in whatever configuration you'd like. — Sarah Aswell.

Nothing gets me and my house in the holiday mood quite like having a few really nice candles ready to go. I stay away from the sweeter smells of Christmas and gravitate for ones like this: evergreen and forest smells that are bright and crisp and cheery (even if you opt for a fake tree for your house). — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that this combines so many of my interests: puzzles, national parks, and advent calendars! I love that this one involves an activity and that it doesn't result in a bunch of cheap junk in your house that never leaves. — Sarah Aswell.

According to recent reports, I love holiday cards, but actually writing them and addressing the envelopes can start to feel like too much of a task, especially with all the other stuff going on around the holidays. I love putting all of my cards, stamps, pens, and stickers in this little case and carrying it with me — I can get a few cards done wherever I am, whether it's my kid's ballet lessons, a doctor's waiting room, or a lunch alone. — Sarah Aswell.

I am really trying to focus my holiday season around activities and togetherness over material things. One great way to do this is to get a few fresh board games that are super family-friendly. I love this one because it is still playable for kids on the younger side, but it's fun for adults, too. It's also just really pretty and magical and fun — you create lovely worlds with cool animals, for points of course. — Sarah Aswell.

Before the holidays start, get yourself a go-to party dress that you can throw on without thinking for whatever occasion. My favorite this season is this dress by Body by Miraclesuit in dark green. You can literally just throw it on and run out the door, and yet it looks so pretty and flattering. And like any good holiday dress, you can elevate it really easily with some heels and jewelry or dress it down with a cardigan and flats. — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that A dull knife is a dangerous knife. This two-sided cylindrical sharpener is a great way to keep your blades in working order. Throw it over a T-shirt and he's ready for dinner without having to change into something stiff.

Industry observers note that there are pants that look good and pants you can comfortably wear on a six-hour flight. Vuori's Meta Pant manages both. The classic five-pocket silhouette looks polished enough for the office or dinner, but the four-way stretch, moisture-wicking fabric, and quick-drying finish make them considerably more forgiving than ordinary trousers. Recent findings suggest that one pair of boots for a rainy commute, a weekend away, and dinner somewhere nice. That's the argument for Blundstone's Heritage #156. Vitamix, the most storied brand in blenders, is becoming a bit more portable. The fresh Nano blends two 20-ounce cups — complete with travel lids — so that you can make a smoothie in the morning, saving your major, overpowered Vitamix for more heavy-duty food prep.

According to recent reports, A man's wallet shouldn't resemble a filing cabinet. Sources indicate that men's jewelry doesn't have to involve leather cords, nautical hardware, or anything resembling a guitar pick. Ian McEwan’s latest novel proves this is the golden age for sci-fi dystopian. Steve McQueen wore Persol 714s. That's a pretty compelling endorsement, even six decades later. No oversize logos, no aggressive wraparound lenses. Just an excellent pair of shades for a man whose taste hasn't been entirely surrendered to practical footwear.

Recent findings suggest that some coffee-table books are glorified furniture. This one earns its space. For the dad who notices the architecture before he notices the menu.

Yes, it's a notebook. A very good one. Leuchtturm1917 gives him 251 numbered pages, a table of contents, two ribbon markers, and binding that lies flat without a wrestling match. For a dad who's spent enough time listening to other people's playlists, here's a way back to his own.

Recent findings suggest that in a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.

Chloe Bridges is an actress with a career spanning film and television. A Columbia University graduate, she welcomed her first child, her son Beau, with her husband, actor and comedian Adam Devine, in February 2024.

It has been revealed that dr. Charis Chambers is a board-certified OBGYN and fellowship-trained pediatric and adolescent gynecologist known to millions online as The Period Doctor. Chloe: I think for me it was that everything is a phase. In the early days, I would get so nervous if something went wrong that day, you know, if he didn’t nap or wasn’t a good sleeper. Sometimes I need help because I can’t be in two places at once. Sometimes I need help because I don’t feel well. Sometimes I need help because I need to be restored, and I need a break. It was an identity shift, but like an identity shift I’d always hoped for but never had the power to change. Becoming a doctor, I knew that. I knew I was going to go to med school. In a recent development, dr. Chambers: RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, is a highly contagious respiratory infection that can get really serious for our youngest babies. When we think about the seasonality of it, it tends to run during the fall and winter months, and the seriousness is that it can lead to hospitalization. It can lead to infant mortality. This is a very serious thing.

Dr. Chambers: Cold and flu can look like fevers and things of that nature. Sometimes it isn’t terribly respiratory leaning. But RSV has a lot to do with how your baby breathes, the retraction signs, and the work of breathing is the term that we use. Babies can get really, really exhausted and tired, and that noisy type of rapid breathing, those are all red flags that something is wrong. These are not all the possible symptoms of RSV in infants, so it’s notable to talk to your doctor. If you notice any symptoms in your baby, talk to your baby’s doctor right away.

Industry observers note that dr. Chambers: During those early months of life, that’s when your baby is at highest risk. Their immune systems are slowly building up, and when we’re thinking about the way RSV might affect an adult, it is not the same for your infant. So if it’s just vaguely on your radar, it’s important to know that this deserves more prioritization. It deserves more energy, more research. If eligible, pregnant women may have the power to help protect their babies by choosing to get vaccinated with ABRYSVO® (Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine), Pfizer’s respiratory syncytial virus vaccine that’s given during 32 through 36 weeks of pregnancy to help protect babies against RSV infection from birth through 6 months during September through January in most of the United States.

To avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age. The most common side effects in pregnant women are injection site pain, headaches, muscle pain, and nausea. Low birth weight and jaundice can also occur in infants. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Chambers: Many moms don’t realize that they are constantly making antibodies to things they’re exposed to and passing those antibodies onto their babies naturally. The RSV vaccination uses that natural process by allowing the mom to create antibodies to RSV and pass them down to her baby. When you get the maternal RSV vaccine, you are helping to protect your baby from the moment they take their first breath. Maternal immunization is an important part of my prenatal care discussions because babies are at highest risk of infection from RSV during their first three months of life.

Chloe: RSV wasn’t on my radar. It was something that I learned about from my OBGYN. ABRYSVO should not be given to anyone with a history of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any of its components. An increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (severe muscle weakness) was observed after vaccination with ABRYSVO. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

Notable Safety Information & Use.

Ask your healthcare provider about the risks and benefits of ABRYSVO. Only a healthcare provider can decide if ABRYSVO is right for you. Always talk to your healthcare provider about any side effects you may experience.

Sources indicate that you are encouraged to report side effects of vaccines to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Visit http://www.vaers.hhs.gov or call 1-800-822-7967.

Individuals who received ABRYSVO during pregnancy are encouraged to enroll in a pregnancy exposure registry at 1-800-616-3791. The registry will monitor pregnancy outcomes.

ABRYSVO is a vaccine indicated for pregnant individuals at 32 through 36 weeks gestational age for the prevention of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and severe LRTD caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants from birth through six months of age.

Please see full Prescribing Information for ABRYSVO at pfi.sr/ABRYSVO_PI.

💡 Key Takeaways
